Where does a team take its shots, and does it make more of them than an average team would from the same spots? This recipe answers both for every field goal attempt of the 2025-26 NBA regular season, with three SportsDataverse packages working together: sportsdataverse-py loads the shots (the stats-API shot file the SportsDataverse publishes on GitHub, so nothing calls stats.nba.com), sdvplot moves them onto sportypy's court and supplies team colors and logos, sportypy draws the court and bins the shots onto it with hexbin. To run it yourself: pip install sportypy sportsdataverse "sdvplot[surfaces]", or from a clone of the repository, uv run --group cookbook jupyter lab. Open in Colab · View the notebook on GitHub import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import polars as pl import sportsdataverse.nba as nba from matplotlib.colors import TwoSlopeNorm import sdvplot from sportypy.surfaces.basketball import NBACourt # print tables as markdown, so the docs site shows them as tables pl.Config.set_tbl_formatting("ASCII_MARKDOWN") pl.Config.set_tbl_hide_column_data_types(True) pl.Config.set_tbl_hide_dataframe_shape(True) SEASON = 2025 # this loader names a season by the year it starts: 2025 is 2025-26
documents.s: Shot quality on an NBA court

documents.t: The stats API reports a shot's location in tenths of a foot with the hoop at the origin. sportypy's court is in feet with the origin at center court. sdvplot.court_coords converts one to the other and adds court_x and court_y; every shot lands on the left half of the court. A shot's value is points when it goes in and 0 when it does not. shots = sdvplot.court_coords( nba.load_nba_stats_shots(seasons=SEASON).filter(pl.col("season_type_id") == "2") # 2: regular season ).with_columns( made=pl.col("shot_result") == "Made", points=pl.when(pl.col("shot_result") == "Made").then(pl.col("shot_value")).otherwise(0), ) print(f"{shots.height:,} shots by {shots['team_tricode'].n_unique()} teams") print(shots.select("team_tricode", "player_name", "shot_value", "shot_distance", "court_x", "court_y", "points").head(3)) 219,159 shots by 30 teams team_tricode player_name shot_value shot_distance court_x court_y points HOU Sengun 3 25 -23.85 -17.9 0 OKC Holmgren 2 1 -40.45 0.0 2 HOU Thompson 3 23 -41.75 23.3 0

NBACourt.hexbin bins the points into hexagons sized in feet (binsize) and clips them to the court. display_range="defense" draws only the left half, where every shot is. The log color scale keeps the rim, which has many times more attempts than anywhere else, from washing out the rest: the rim, the corners and the arc are the darkest, and the long two in between takes about a tenth as many shots as the arc. court = NBACourt() fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 6.5)) court.draw(ax=ax, display_range="defense") hexes = court.hexbin(shots["court_x"], shots["court_y"], binsize=1.5, bins="log", cmap="magma_r", mincnt=1, ax=ax) fig.colorbar(hexes, ax=ax, shrink=0.6, pad=0.02, label="Attempts (log scale)") ax.set_title(f"All {shots.height:,} NBA field goal attempts, 2025-26 regular season", loc="left", fontweight="bold") fig.text(0.99, 0.01, "Data: NBA stats API shot file via sportsdataverse-py", ha="right", fontsize=8, color="grey") plt.show()

The league's average points per attempt at each distance (in whole feet, with everything past 35 feet pooled) and shot value is the baseline for the rest of the recipe: an average team's expected return on the same shot. A two at the rim is worth well over a point; the long two is the worst shot on the floor, and a step back behind the arc is worth more than a step in. expected = ( shots.with_columns(dist=pl.col("shot_distance").clip(upper_bound=35)) .group_by("dist", "shot_value") .agg(attempts=pl.len(), xpts=pl.col("points").mean()) .filter(pl.col("attempts") >= 50) .sort("dist") ) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4)) for value, color in ((2, "#006838"), (3, "#e06000")): line = expected.filter(pl.col("shot_value") == value) ax.plot(line["dist"], line["xpts"], marker="o", ms=3, color=color, label=f"{value}-point attempts") ax.axhline(shots["points"].mean(), color="grey", lw=0.8, ls="--", label="League average, all shots") ax.set(xlabel="Shot distance (ft)", ylabel="Points per attempt", ylim=(0, None)) ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False) ax.legend(frameon=False) ax.set_title("Points per attempt by distance, 2025-26", loc="left", fontweight="bold") plt.show()
documents.s: 3. What a shot is worth from each distance

documents.t: Join the baseline back onto every shot and each one gets an expected value, xpts. A make from a spot where the league scores 1.1 points per attempt is worth 2 - 1.1 = +0.9 over expected, a miss there -1.1. Summed over a season, that separates teams that take good shots (a high xpts per attempt) from teams that make the shots they take (a high over per attempt). shots = shots.with_columns(dist=pl.col("shot_distance").clip(upper_bound=35)).join( expected.select("dist", "shot_value", "xpts"), on=["dist", "shot_value"], how="left" ).with_columns(over=pl.col("points") - pl.col("xpts")) teams = ( shots.drop_nulls("xpts") .group_by("team_tricode") .agg(attempts=pl.len(), pts=pl.col("points").mean(), xpts=pl.col("xpts").mean(), over=pl.col("over").mean()) .sort("over", descending=True) ) with pl.Config(float_precision=3, tbl_rows=10): print(pl.concat([teams.head(5), teams.tail(5)])) team_tricode attempts pts xpts over LAL 6863 1.146 1.069 0.077 DEN 7196 1.154 1.079 0.075 BOS 7398 1.106 1.052 0.053 LAC 6857 1.118 1.072 0.045 MIL 7012 1.131 1.093 0.037 PHI 7404 1.061 1.098 -0.037 CHI 7417 1.095 1.146 -0.051 POR 7389 1.067 1.119 -0.051 BKN 6933 1.041 1.106 -0.065 NOP 7420 1.054 1.122 -0.068
documents.s: 4. Points over expected, shot by shot

documents.t: Pass over as the hexbin's values and each hexagon shows the team's average points over expected there (mincnt leaves out spots with too few attempts to say). A diverging palette centered on zero puts the league average in white. The courts are painted in each team's colors from sdvplot (team_colors), handed to sportypy as color_updates, and add_logos puts the team's logo beyond the arc. best, worst = teams["team_tricode"][0], teams["team_tricode"][-1] norm = TwoSlopeNorm(vcenter=0, vmin=-0.6, vmax=0.6) fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5.4)) for ax, team in zip(axes, (best, worst)): primary = sdvplot.team_colors("nba", team) secondary = sdvplot.team_colors("nba", team, which="secondary") court = NBACourt(color_updates={"court_apron": primary, "center_circle_fill": secondary}) court.draw(ax=ax, display_range="defense") mine = shots.filter((pl.col("team_tricode") == team) & pl.col("over").is_not_null()) hexes = court.hexbin(mine["court_x"], mine["court_y"], values=mine["over"], binsize=4, mincnt=20, cmap="RdBu_r", norm=norm, edgecolors="white", linewidths=0.3, ax=ax) sdvplot.add_logos(ax, [-12], [0], [team], league="nba", height=0.12, zorder=30) row = teams.filter(pl.col("team_tricode") == team).row(0, named=True) ax.set_title(f"{team}: {row['over']:+.3f} points per shot over expected", loc="left", fontsize=10) fig.colorbar(hexes, ax=axes, shrink=0.6, pad=0.02, label="Points over expected per attempt") fig.suptitle("The best and worst shooting teams of 2025-26, spot by spot", x=0.01, ha="left", fontweight="bold") fig.text(0.99, 0.01, "Data: NBA stats API shot file via sportsdataverse-py", ha="right", fontsize=8, color="grey") plt.show()

documents.t: The NBACourt reference lists every feature color_updates can repaint, and the plotting reference every option of hexbin, heatmap and contour. sdvplot's surfaces and shot charts cookbook draws single-player shot charts on team-colored courts in one call. Swap nba for wnba (load_wnba_stats_shots, sdvplot.court_coords and sportypy's WNBACourt) and the recipe runs unchanged on the WNBA.

A shot from the slot goes in far more often than one from the point. Expected goals (xG) puts a number on that: the chance an average shooter scores from where, and how, a shot was taken. This recipe maps the 2025-26 NHL regular season onto sportypy's rink with three SportsDataverse packages: sportsdataverse-py loads fastRhockey's play-by-play, whose xg column is fastRhockey's expected goals model, sportypy draws the rink and bins the shots with heatmap, sdvplot supplies team colors and logos. To run it yourself: pip install sportypy sportsdataverse "sdvplot[surfaces]", or from a clone of the repository, uv run --group cookbook jupyter lab. Open in Colab · View the notebook on GitHub import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import polars as pl import sportsdataverse.nhl as nhl from matplotlib.colors import TwoSlopeNorm import sdvplot from sportypy.surfaces.hockey import NHLRink # print tables as markdown, so the docs site shows them as tables pl.Config.set_tbl_formatting("ASCII_MARKDOWN") pl.Config.set_tbl_hide_column_data_types(True) pl.Config.set_tbl_hide_dataframe_shape(True) SEASON = 2026 # this loader names a season by the year it ends: 2026 is 2025-26
documents.s: Expected goals on an NHL rink

documents.t: fastRhockey's x_fixed and y_fixed are in feet on the NHL rink's frame, the one sportypy draws, with the origin at center ice. Shots on goal, misses and goals are the unblocked attempts (a blocked shot is recorded where it was blocked, not where it was taken). Empty-net goals are left out: they say nothing about shooting. Mirroring the shots at the left net (flipping both signs) puts every attempt at the right one. pbp = nhl.load_nhl_pbp_lite(seasons=[SEASON]) shots = ( pbp.filter( pl.col("event_type").is_in(["SHOT", "MISSED_SHOT", "GOAL"]) & (pl.col("season_type") == "R") & ~pl.col("empty_net") & pl.col("xg").is_not_null() ) .with_columns( x=pl.col("x_fixed").abs(), y=pl.when(pl.col("x_fixed") < 0).then(-pl.col("y_fixed")).otherwise(pl.col("y_fixed")), goal=pl.col("event_type") == "GOAL", ) .filter(pl.col("x") > 25) # the offensive zone (the blue line is 25 ft from center) ) games = pbp.filter(pl.col("season_type") == "R")["game_id"].n_unique() print(f"{shots.height:,} unblocked shots and {shots['goal'].sum():,} goals in {games:,} games") 106,733 unblocked shots and 7,390 goals in 1,312 games
documents.s: 1. Every unblocked shot, at one net

documents.t: Two views of the same shots on the attacking half (display_range="offense"). On the left, heatmap counts the attempts in 3-foot squares. On the right, statistic="mean" with values=goal turns each square into a shooting percentage, with squares of fewer than 25 attempts left blank. Shots come from everywhere in the zone; goals come from the slot and the crease. fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5.5)) rink = NHLRink() rink.draw(ax=axes[0], display_range="offense") counts = rink.heatmap(shots["x"], shots["y"], binsize=3, cmap="Blues", ax=axes[0]) fig.colorbar(counts, ax=axes[0], shrink=0.7, pad=0.02, label="Unblocked attempts") axes[0].set_title("Where shots come from", loc="left", fontweight="bold") rink.draw(ax=axes[1], display_range="offense") rate = rink.heatmap(shots["x"], shots["y"], values=shots["goal"].cast(pl.Float64), binsize=3, statistic=lambda g: g.mean() if len(g) >= 25 else np.nan, cmap="Reds", vmin=0, vmax=0.3, ax=axes[1]) fig.colorbar(rate, ax=axes[1], shrink=0.7, pad=0.02, label="Shooting percentage") axes[1].set_title("Where goals come from", loc="left", fontweight="bold") fig.text(0.99, 0.02, "Data: fastRhockey via sportsdataverse-py", ha="right", fontsize=8, color="grey") plt.show()
documents.s: 2. Where shots come from, and where goals come from

documents.t: A good xG model is honest: of the shots it gives a 10% chance, about 10% should go in. Group the shots by their xg into ten equal-sized deciles and compare the average expected goal with the share that actually scored. calibration = ( shots.with_columns(decile=(pl.col("xg").rank("ordinal") * 10 / pl.len()).ceil().cast(pl.Int8)) .group_by("decile") .agg(shots=pl.len(), expected=pl.col("xg").mean(), actual=pl.col("goal").mean()) .sort("decile") ) with pl.Config(float_precision=3): print(calibration) print(f"Season: {shots['xg'].sum():,.0f} expected goals, {shots['goal'].sum():,} scored") decile shots expected actual 1 10673 0.007 0.007 2 10673 0.015 0.012 3 10673 0.024 0.017 4 10674 0.036 0.027 5 10673 0.049 0.038 6 10673 0.064 0.053 7 10674 0.084 0.077 8 10673 0.109 0.101 9 10673 0.147 0.137 10 10674 0.237 0.224 Season: 8,243 expected goals, 7,390 scored Every decile scores more often than the one before it, so the model ranks shots well. But almost every decile comes in under its expected rate: over 2025-26 the model ran about 10% high, 8,243 expected goals for 7,390 scored. The goals above expected in section 5 are measured against it, so a league-average finisher sits a little below zero.
documents.s: 3. Is the expected goals model calibrated?

documents.t: Which spots does a team shoot from more often than the league? heatmap sums its values, so one call can take the difference: give each of the team's shots +1 / its games and each league shot -1 / every team's games, and each square shows how many more (red) or fewer (blue) attempts per game the team takes there than an average team. The team is the one with the most expected goals, its rink's boards painted in its sdvplot color. team_xg = shots.group_by("event_team_abbr").agg(xg=pl.col("xg").sum()).sort("xg", descending=True) team = team_xg["event_team_abbr"][0] team_games = pbp.filter( (pl.col("season_type") == "R") & ((pl.col("home_abbr") == team) | (pl.col("away_abbr") == team)) )["game_id"].n_unique() mine = shots.filter(pl.col("event_team_abbr") == team) x = pl.concat([mine["x"], shots["x"]]) y = pl.concat([mine["y"], shots["y"]]) weights = np.concatenate([np.full(mine.height, 1 / team_games), np.full(shots.height, -1 / (2 * games))]) primary = sdvplot.team_colors("nhl", team) rink = NHLRink(color_updates={"boards": primary}) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6.5)) rink.draw(ax=ax, display_range="offense") diff = rink.heatmap(x, y, values=weights, binsize=8, cmap="RdBu_r", norm=TwoSlopeNorm(0, -0.4, 0.4), ax=ax) fig.colorbar(diff, ax=ax, shrink=0.6, pad=0.02, label="Attempts per game above the league average") sdvplot.add_logos(ax, [12], [0], [team], league="nhl", height=0.16, zorder=30) ax.set_title(f"{team}: the NHL's most expected goals in 2025-26 ({team_xg['xg'][0] / team_games:.2f} per game)", loc="left", fontweight="bold") fig.text(0.99, 0.01, "Data: fastRhockey via sportsdataverse-py", ha="right", fontsize=8, color="grey") plt.show()

documents.t: Goals above expected is a player's goals minus the expected goals of their shots: how many more they scored than an average shooter would have from the same chances. The NHLRink reference lists every feature color_updates can repaint, and the plotting reference every option of heatmap, hexbin, contour and scatter. sportypy draws the other leagues' rinks too (AHLRink, PHFRink, IIHFRink, NCAARink and more); their frames match, so the recipe needs only a different rink and data source. sdvplot's surfaces and shot charts cookbook draws a single player's goals on a team-colored rink in one call.

Each league that is supported by sportypy has its own class in its respective sport under the surfaces submodule. The one exception is high school football: the 11-, 9-, 8- and 6-player NFHS fields are all NFHSField, chosen with n_players (see Surface Units below). As an example, you can instantiate an NHL rink like so: # Load from the hockey submodule in surfaces from sportypy.surfaces.hockey import NHLRink # Create the NHL rink nhl = NHLRink() If you want to see what this would yield, you may call the draw() method that belongs to each league surface, like so: # Draw the NHL rink nhl.draw() Each league's class may take on the following arguments when it is created: {surface_type}_updates (rink_updates, court_updates, field_updates, pitch_updates or sheet_updates, depending on the sport): A dictionary of updates to the parameters that define the surface. To get the list of parameters you can change, run cani_change_dimensions() on your league's surface color_updates: A dictionary of updates to the features' colors on the plot. These are named by what the feature is, using snake_case to specify the names. To get the list of color names you can change, run cani_color_features() on your league's surface (e.g. NHLRink().cani_color_features()) rotation: An angle (in degrees) that you'd like to rotate the plot by, where +θ is counterclockwise x_trans and y_trans: By default, the origin of the coordinate system always lies at the center of the plot. For example, (0.0, 0.0) on a basketball court lies along the division line and on the line that connects the center of each basket. If you want to shift the origin (and therefore the entire plot), use x_trans and y_trans to do so units: If your data is in units that are different than how the rule book of the league specifies the units (e.g. you've got NHL data in inches, but the rule book describes the rink in feet), set this to the units you've got your data in, as in NHLRink(units = "in"). You're welcome to change the units of the data as well, but this is provided for convenience The draw() method then takes: ax: The matplotlib.Axes object to draw on (a new figure is created if you don't pass one). draw() returns the Axes it drew on display_range: This automatically "zooms" in on the area of the plot you're interested in. Valid ranges here vary by sport, and are listed for each sport in the API reference xlim and ylim: Any limits you'd like to put on the plot in the x and y direction. These will overwrite anything set by the display_range parameter rotation: An angle (in degrees) to rotate this drawing by, in place of the surface's own rotation cani_plot_leagues() lists the leagues that a sport's surface can be drawn for. Some class names exist in several sports (e.g. NCAACourt in basketball, tennis and volleyball; NCAAField and NFHSField in baseball and football). The package-level sportypy.surfaces.<name> resolves to only one of them, so always import colliding names from their sport module, e.g. from sportypy.surfaces.volleyball import NCAACourt.

All of the draw() methods, by default, will draw the surface in what can be considered "TV view", or the way that the surface would typically be displayed on a television broadcast. This typically means the action moves from left to right across the screen (a basketball game that has the baskets on the left and right end of the court). As mentioned above, it is possible to change this to be in any orientation through the rotation parameter to each draw() method. There are a few exceptions to this: {baseball league}Field plots are displayed from the high-home view by default, as baseball coordinates typically have the +y axis extending from the back tip of home plate towards center field {tennis league}Court is displayed with the court diagrammed from the perspective of the chair umpire

Related to the idea of custom displays of the plot is the concept of the display_range parameter in the league's class draw() method. This is unique to each sport, but globally supported across the package. This parameter allows the specification of a designated region of the surface to display. As an example, if you're trying to limit the analysis of NFL data to being inside of the red zone, you may want to do something similar to the following: # Import football fields from sportypy.surfaces.football import NFLField # Draw the red zone of an NFL field NFLField().draw(display_range = "red zone") Another use case would be to make the data you're viewing easier to see. Say you wanted to look at curling data, but only cared about stone positions in the house (and not the path as to how the stones got there). You might do this: # Import the curling sheets from sportypy.surfaces.curling import WCFSheet # Draw only the house of a curling sheet WCFSheet().draw(display_range = "house")

Each league's surface has a standardized unit of measure in which the plot is created, and is standardized by the primary units specified in their respective rule books. They are as follows (and any explanation is in parentheses): Sport League Primary Plotting Unit Baseball Little League ft Baseball MiLB ft Baseball MLB ft Baseball NCAA ft Baseball NFHS (High School) ft Baseball Pony ft Basketball FIBA m Basketball NBA ft Basketball NBA G League ft Basketball NCAA ft Basketball NFHS ft Basketball WNBA ft Curling Curling Canada ft Curling WCF (World Curling Federation) ft Football CFL yd Football NCAA yd Football NFHS11 (High School, 11 players) yd Football NFHS6 (High School, 6 players) yd Football NFHS8 (High School, 8 players) yd Football NFHS9 (High School, 9 players) yd Football NFL yd Hockey AHL ft Hockey ECHL ft Hockey IIHF m Hockey NCAA ft Hockey NHL ft Hockey NWHL ft Hockey OHL ft Hockey PHF ft Hockey PWHL ft Hockey QMJHL ft Hockey USHL ft Lacrosse NCAA (Men's) yd Lacrosse NCAA (Women's) m Lacrosse NLL (box lacrosse) ft Lacrosse PLL yd Lacrosse USA Lacrosse (Men's) yd Lacrosse USA Lacrosse (Women's) m Lacrosse World Lacrosse (box) ft Soccer EPL m Soccer FIFA m Soccer MLS yd Soccer NCAA yd Soccer NWSL yd Softball NCAA ft Tennis ATP ft Tennis ITA ft Tennis ITF ft Tennis NCAA ft Tennis USTA ft Tennis WTA ft Volleyball FIVB m Volleyball NCAA m Volleyball USA Volleyball m The four NFHS football fields share the NFHSField class: NFHSField() draws the 11-player field, and NFHSField(n_players = 9), NFHSField(n_players = 8) and NFHSField(n_players = 6) draw the others. # Draw a 6-player high school football field from sportypy.surfaces.football import NFHSField NFHSField(n_players = 6).draw() However, since the data that is supplied may come in various units of measure, the plots are able to be generated in the data's units. This is done with the units argument to the class constructor, or via the {surface_name}_updates attribute in the class constructor, using the {surface_name}_units key (e.g. NHLRink(rink_updates = {"rink_units": "in"})). The features themselves will look visually identical, but the underlying coordinate grid will change.

Some examples to help navigate the package: # Draw an NBA court from sportypy.surfaces.basketball import NBACourt NBACourt().draw() # Customize a college basketball court to replicate that of the University of # Illinois Fighting Illini from sportypy.surfaces.basketball import NCAACourt NCAACourt( color_updates = { "offensive_half_court": "#e8e0d7", "defensive_half_court": "#e8e0d7", "court_apron": "#e84a27", "two_point_range": ["#e8e0d7", "#ffffff66"], "center_circle_fill": "#e8e0d7", "painted_area": "#e84a27", "free_throw_circle_fill": "#e8e0d7", "sideline": "#13294b", "endline": "#13294b", "division_line": "#13294b", "center_circle_outline": "#13294b", "lane_boundary": ["#ffffff", "#ffffff00"], "three_point_line": ["#13294b", "#ffffff"], "free_throw_circle_outline": "#ffffff", "lane_space_mark": "#ffffff", "restricted_arc": "#13294b", "backboard": "#13294b" } ).draw()

In addition to just creating the baseline plots, sportypy has several methods to display analyses on top of the surfaces that the classes create. The syntax is meant to wrap matplotlib methods. Due to the nature of the layering of the surface's features, it's recommended to use the zorder parameter in the range of 11 to 15 to display model outputs, and zorder >= 20 to display individual tracking data points. This allows the features of the surface to be displayed when plotting models while also representing a birds-eye view of any action on the surface (e.g. player positions). The first two examples use the Big Data Cup 2021 data from the 2021 NWHL season (the league became the PHF later that year). # Plot shot locations provided by the Big Data Cup # Import packages import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd from sportypy.surfaces.hockey import PHFRink # Download the data bdc = pd.read_csv( "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bigdatacup/Big-Data-Cup-2021/" "main/hackathon_nwhl.csv" ) # Select the Minnesota Whitecaps vs. Boston Pride game (first game in sample) bdc = bdc.loc[ (bdc["Home Team"] == "Minnesota Whitecaps") & (bdc["Away Team"] == "Boston Pride") ] # Filter to only be shots shots = bdc.loc[bdc["Event"].isin(["Shot", "Goal"])] # Separate shots by team bos_shots = shots[shots["Team"] == "Boston Pride"] min_shots = shots[shots["Team"] == "Minnesota Whitecaps"] # Instantiate a PHF rink, adjusting the coordinates to match the data # (The coordinate (0, 0) is in the bottom-left of the plot) phf = PHFRink(x_trans = 100.0, y_trans = 42.5) # Draw the rink on a matplotlib.Axes object fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1) phf.draw(ax = ax) # Add the plot of each team's shots phf.scatter( bos_shots["X Coordinate"], bos_shots["Y Coordinate"], color = "#fec52e" ) phf.scatter( 200.0 - min_shots["X Coordinate"], 85.0 - min_shots["Y Coordinate"], color = "#2251b8" ) The Whitecaps shots are on the left side. To add team colors and logos, see sdvplot. # Show passing start/end locations with an arrow plot # Import packages import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd from sportypy.surfaces.hockey import PHFRink # Download the same Big Data Cup data as above bdc = pd.read_csv( "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bigdatacup/Big-Data-Cup-2021/" "main/hackathon_nwhl.csv" ) bdc = bdc.loc[ (bdc["Home Team"] == "Minnesota Whitecaps") & (bdc["Away Team"] == "Boston Pride") ] # Filter to only be Boston's passes passes = bdc.loc[ (bdc["Team"] == "Boston Pride") & (bdc["Event"] == "Play") ] # Instantiate a PHF rink, adjusting the coordinates to match the data # (The coordinate (0, 0) is in the bottom-left of the plot) phf = PHFRink(x_trans = 100.0, y_trans = 42.5) # Draw the rink on a matplotlib.Axes object fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1) phf.draw(ax = ax) # Add the arrow plot of Boston's passes phf.arrow( passes["X Coordinate"], passes["Y Coordinate"], passes["X Coordinate 2"], passes["Y Coordinate 2"], color = "#ffcb05" ) The next two examples load their data with sportsdataverse-py (pip install sportsdataverse), which reads the files the SportsDataverse publishes on GitHub, and work with polars frames, which it returns. The cookbooks take both further. # This example is adapted from the hockey_rink package's documentation, which # can be found here: https://github.com/the-bucketless/hockey_rink#examples # Import packages import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import polars as pl import sportsdataverse.nhl as nhl from sportypy.surfaces.hockey import NHLRink # Load the 2019-20 NHL play-by-play (fastRhockey's, through sportsdataverse-py; # this loader names a season by the year it ends) pbp = nhl.load_nhl_pbp_lite(seasons = [2020]) # Keep the unblocked shots (shots on goal, misses and goals) with a location pbp = pbp.filter( pl.col("event_type").is_in(["SHOT", "MISSED_SHOT", "GOAL"]) & pl.col("x_fixed").is_not_null() & pl.col("y_fixed").is_not_null() ) # x_fixed and y_fixed are in feet on the NHL rink, with the origin at center # ice. Force all x coordinates to be on the same side of the ice, and adjust # the y coordinates so the shots are from the same direction pbp = pbp.with_columns( x = pl.col("x_fixed").abs(), y = pl.col("y_fixed") * pl.col("x_fixed").sign(), goal = (pl.col("event_type") == "GOAL").cast(pl.Int8) ) # Subset to only shots in the offensive zone (the blue line is 25 ft from # center ice) pbp = pbp.filter(pl.col("x") > 25) # Create a matplotlib.Axes object for the test plots to lie on fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize = (14, 8)) # Instantiate an NHL rink nhl_rink = NHLRink() # Draw a rink on each of the three matplotlib.Axes objects defined above # and subset them to only the offensive zone for i in range(3): nhl_rink.draw(ax = axs[i], display_range = "ozone") # Add the contour plot contour_img = nhl_rink.contourf( pbp["x"], pbp["y"], values = pbp["goal"], ax = axs[0], cmap = "bwr", plot_range = "ozone", binsize = 10, levels = 50, statistic = "mean" ) # Add a colorbar legend to the bottom to make the metrics easier to read plt.colorbar(contour_img, ax = axs[0], orientation = "horizontal") # Add the heatmap plot nhl_rink.heatmap( pbp["x"], pbp["y"], values = pbp["goal"], ax = axs[1], cmap = "magma", plot_xlim = (25, 89), # offensive-side blue line to the goal line statistic = "mean", vmax = 0.2, binsize = 3 ) # Add the hexbin plot nhl_rink.hexbin( pbp["x"], pbp["y"], values = pbp["goal"], ax = axs[2], binsize = (8, 12), plot_range = "ozone", zorder = 25, alpha = 0.85 ) # Create an NBA shot heat map. The example below uses Ayo Dosunmu's rookie # season # Import packages import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import polars as pl import sportsdataverse.nba as nba from sportypy.surfaces.basketball import NBACourt # Load the 2021-22 NBA stats API shots (the shot file the SportsDataverse # publishes, through sportsdataverse-py; this loader names a season by the # year it starts), and keep Ayo Dosunmu's regular-season shots shot_data = nba.load_nba_stats_shots(seasons = 2021).filter( (pl.col("person_id") == 1630245) & (pl.col("season_type_id") == "2") ) # x_legacy and y_legacy are the stats API's LOC_X and LOC_Y: tenths of a foot, # with the basket at the origin. Rotate them by 90 degrees to align with the # sportypy convention, and divide by 10 to get feet shot_data = shot_data.with_columns( x = -pl.col("y_legacy") / 10.0, y = pl.col("x_legacy") / 10.0, shot_made = (pl.col("shot_result") == "Made").cast(pl.Int8) ) # Define the matplotlib instances to plot onto fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1) # Start by instantiating a court class. NBA shot data is what's used, so an # NBA court is selected. Shifting the court by the basket's distance from # center court puts the right-hand basket at the data's origin, and the # "offense" display range shows only that half nba_court = NBACourt(x_trans = -41.75) nba_court.draw(ax = ax, display_range = "offense") nba_court.heatmap( shot_data["x"], shot_data["y"], values = shot_data["shot_made"], ax = ax, alpha = 0.75, cmap = "hot" )

sportypy draws regulation, to-scale playing surfaces with matplotlib, so tracking and play-by-play data can be plotted on the field, court, rink or sheet it came from. It covers baseball, basketball, curling, football, hockey, lacrosse, soccer, softball, tennis and volleyball, with a class for each league's rule-book dimensions. It is the Python counterpart of sportyR and keeps parity with it: the same leagues, dimensions, colors and display ranges. For JavaScript and TypeScript, @sportsdataverse/sporty is the port of both.
sportypy supports Python 3.10 and newer. pip install sportypy or, in a uv project, uv add sportypy
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sportypy.surfaces.hockey import NHLRink NHLRink().draw() plt.show()

The features a baseball surface is drawn from (sportypy._feature_classes.baseball).

An extension of the BaseFeature class for baseball features. The following attributes are specific to baseball features only. For more information on inherited attributes, please see the BaseFeature class definition. The default values are provided to ensure that the feature can at least be created.

feature_radius (float): The radius needed to draw the feature. This may not be needed for all features. The default is 0.0 feature_thickness (float): The thickness with which to draw the feature. This is normally given as the horizontal width of the feature in TV view, however it may be used to specify other thicknesses as needed. The default is 0.0 field_units (str): The units with which the feature is drawn. The default is "ft"
The constraint around the bounding box of the field. This can be a bit tricky, so large default values are set here.

The dirt that comprises the infield. This includes the base paths, the infield arc, and the home plate circle. The home plate circle may be drawn over in other shapes as needed (example: Detroit's Comerica Park has a home plate shaped dirt area as the home plate "circle")

home_plate_circle_radius (float): The radius of the dirt circle surrounding home plate foul_line_to_foul_grass (float): The distance from the outer edge of the foul line to the inner edge of the grass in foul territory pitchers_plate_dist (float): The distance from the front edge of the pitcher's plate to the back tip of home plate infield_arc_radius (float): The distance from the front edge of the pitcher's mound to the back of the infield dirt

Home plate. The back tip of home plate will be located at the origin.

A base on the diamond. The base is where a runner is considered safe

The lines that designate fair territory from foul territory. Since a ball on the line is considered in fair territory, the outer edge of the baseline must lie in fair territory (aka the line y = +/- x)

As an example, if the base lines are 90 feet, and the running lane starts a distance of 45 feet down the line from the back tip of home plate, and extends 3 feet beyond first base, this parameter would be given as 48.0 running_lane_depth (float): The straight-line distance from the outer edge of the first-base line to the outer edge of the running lane running_lane_start_distance (float): The straight-line distance from the back tip of home plate to the start of the running lane
The features a basketball surface is drawn from (sportypy._feature_classes.basketball).

An extension of the BaseFeature class for basketball features. The following attributes are specific to basketball features only. For more information on inherited attributes, please see the BaseFeature class definition. The default values are provided to ensure that the feature can at least be created.

court_length (float): The length of the court in TV view. The default is 0.0 court_width (float): The width of the court in TV view. The default is 0.0 feature_radius (float): The radius needed to draw the feature. This may not be needed for all features. The default is 0.0 feature_thickness (float): The thickness with which to draw the feature. This is normally given as the horizontal width of the feature in TV view, however it may be used to specify other thicknesses as needed. The default is 0.0 field_units (str): The units with which the feature is drawn. The default is "ft"
The constraint around the interior edge of the court's boundary lines. This confines all interior features to be constrained inside the court, as well as any interior plots.
One half of the basketball court. Each half court spans from the inner edge of the baseline to the center of the division line, and serves as the base layer of the court
The apron of the court. The apron is the colored boundary around the exterior of some courts. If no such colored boundary exists, this should take the same color as the court floor

court_apron_endline (float): The thickness of the court's apron beyond the endline court_apron_sideline (float): The thickness of the court's apron beyond the sideline court_apron_to_boundary (float): The distance from the inner edge of the court apron to the outer edge of the court's boundary line (sideline and endline will be spaced the same)

The outline of the circle(s) at the center of the court. The circle is where the tip-off to the game takes place. The supplied radius (radii) should be measured to the outside of the circle, with the center of the circle(s) being the exact center of the court

The interior of the circle(s) at the center of the court. The circle is where the tip-off to the game takes place. The supplied radius (radii) should be measured to the outside of the circle, with the center of the circle(s) being the exact center of the court

The center court line. This line divides the court in half, and is sometimes referred to as the time line or half-court line. The center of this line goes through the y axis, with half of the line lying in a team's offensive half court and the other half in their defensive half court
division_line_extension (float): The distance that the division line extends beyond the sidelines. This may be omitted if the value is 0
The area of the court where made baskets are worth two points. This is the area enclosed by the three-point line's outer edge and the baseline's inner edge

basket_center_to_baseline (float): The distance from the center of the basket ring to the inner edge of the baseline basket_center_to_corner_three (float): The distance from the center of the basket ring to the outer edge of the three-point line in the corner

The line separating two-point range from three-point range. Made shots inside this line count for two points, and made shots from beyond this line are worth three points. The radius of the feature should be to its exterior

basket_center_to_baseline (float): The distance from the center of the basket ring to the inner edge of the baseline basket_center_to_corner_three (float): The distance from the center of the basket ring to the outer edge of the three-point line in the corner
The painted area inside the free-throw lane. The painted area may have a margin from the interior edges of the free throw lane, although this margin will default to 0.0 units

lane_length (float): The distance from the inner edge of the baseline to the center-court side of the free-throw lane in TV view lane_width (float): The distance from the outer edges of the free-throw lane when viewing the court in TV view paint_margin (float): The distance from the painted area of the lane to the lane boundary lines

The outline of the free-throw lane. The lines providing the boundary to the free-throw lane. When a player is shooting a free-throw, all non-shooting players must be outside of this boundary. NOTE: This does not include lane space markings (blocks), which will be created via the LaneSpaceMark class

lane_length (float): The distance from the inner edge of the baseline to the center-court side of the free-throw lane in TV view lane_width (float): The distance from the outer edges of the free-throw lane when viewing the court in TV view
The filling of the area where a play shoots a free-throw. The provided radius should be to the free-throw circle's exterior
The outline of the circle around the free-throw line. The provided radius should be to the free-throw circle's exterior

The lane space marks (blocks) on the outside of the free-throw lane. These are the marks where non-shooting players stand during free-throws. Players may not cross these lines before the ball touches the rim on the shot attempt
mark_depth (float): The length (measurement in the baseline-to-free-throw-line direction) of lane space marks (blocks) of the free-throw lane
The endlines on the basketball court. These are sometimes referred to as the baselines, and are located beyond each basket
The sidelines on the basketball court. These are the lines that run the full length of the court, typically with the team bench areas and substitution areas on their exterior

The inbounding line. This is where the ball is inbounded on the sideline when necessary. Lines drawn on the top of the court should be drawn in a top-down direction, and lines on the bottom of the court should be drawn in the bottom-up direction

in_play_ext (float): The distance into the court (measured from the inner edge of the sideline) that the inbounding lines protrude into the court out_of_bounds_ext (float): The distance away from the court (measured from the outer edge of the sideline) that the inbounding lines protrude away the court drawn_direction (str): The direction in which to draw the inbounding line

The substitution lines. This is where players checking into the game wait for a stoppage. Lines drawn on the top of the court should be drawn in a top-down direction, and lines on the bottom of the court should be drawn in the bottom-up direction

substitution_line_width (float): The distance away from the court (measured from the outer edge of the sideline) that the substitution lines protrude away from the court drawn_direction (str): The direction in which to draw the substitution line

The lower defensive box marks. The lower defensive box is an imaginary box on the court extending from the lines on the baseline to the lines inside the painted area. extension (float): The distance that the lower defensive box markings extend from their anchor points drawn_direction (str): The direction in which to draw the lower defensive box mark

extension (float): The distance that the team bench line extends from its anchor point drawn_direction (str): The direction in which to draw the lower defensive box mark

The backboard. This is the backing onto which the basket ring (created separately) is affixed
backboard_thickness (float): The thickness of the backboard. This is the observed thickness when viewing the court from a bird's eye view
The basket ring. The hoop through which the ball must pass to score points for a team

basket_ring_connector_extension (float): The distance the basket ring's connector extends from the backboard into the free-throw lane basket_ring_connector_width (float): The dimension of the piece of the basket ring that connects the backboard to the basket ring. A parameterization of a single ring in the house. The rings are concentric, centered at the intersection of the tee line and centre line

The features a hockey surface is drawn from (sportypy._feature_classes.hockey).

An extension of the BaseFeature class for hockey features. The following attributes are specific to hockey features only. For more information on inherited attributes, please see the BaseFeature class definition. The default values are provided to ensure that the feature can at least be created.

rink_length (float): The length of the rink in TV view. The default is 0.0 rink_width (float): The width of the rink in TV view. The default is 0.0 feature_radius (float): The radius needed to draw the feature. This may not be needed for all features. The default is 0.0 feature_thickness (float): The thickness with which to draw the feature. This is normally given as the horizontal width of the feature in TV view, however it may be used to specify other thicknesses as needed. The default is 0.0 field_units (str): The units with which the feature is drawn. The default is "ft"

A parameterization of the boards of a hockey rink. The method below specifies one half of the rink's boards. The rest of the boards are produced via a reflection over the x-axis when viewing the rink in TV view. The rink's boards are rounded in the arc of a circle of a specified radius, so the x and y coordinates of its center must be taken and shifted to their correct location on the ice surface

A parameterization of the constraint of the boards of a hockey rink. This corresponds to the inner edges of the boards and is used to constrain other features from extending beyond the inner boundary of the ice rink. Unlike the Boards class (defined above), this feature is designed to function over the entire surface of an ice rink
A parameterization of the defensive zone of a hockey rink. The offensive zone is the left "third" of the rink in TV view. This is the area that a team defends when attacking from left to right
nzone_length (float): The length of the neutral zone, measured from the interior edges of the zone lines (blue lines)

A parameterization of the neutral zone of a hockey rink. The neutral zone is the middle "third" of the rink. This is the area between the two zone (blue) lines. The center of the neutral zone should lie along the line x = 0

A parameterization of the offensive zone of a hockey rink. The offensive zone is the right "third" of the rink in TV view. This is the area that a team attacks to try to score a goal when attacking from left to right
nzone_length (float): The length of the neutral zone, measured from the interior edges of the zone lines (blue lines)

A parameterization of the center line of a hockey rink. The center line is the line that divides the ice surface in half. Its center should lie directly in the center of the ice surface. Its line thickness should be given by major_line_thickness as this is a major line on the ice surface
center_faceoff_spot_gap (float): The gap in the center line that surrounds the center faceoff spot. This is measured between the inner edges of the two halves of the center line
A parameterization of the referee's crease. The referee's crease is a semi-circle on the "bottom" of the boards (in TV view), centered on the line y = 0 (the center of the center line)

A parameterization of the center faceoff spot of a hockey rink. The center faceoff spot is the spot at which the game begins. Its center should lie directly in the center of the ice surface. Its radius is passed as a key in rink_params

A parameterization of the zone lines of a hockey rink. The zone lines are the lines that separate the neutral zone from the offensive and defensive zones. Its line thickness should be given by major_line_thickness as this is a major line on the ice surface

A parameterization of the goal lines of a hockey rink. The goal lines are the lines over which a puck must cross (within the goal frame) in order to be considered a goal. Its line thickness should be given by minor_line_thickness as this is a minor line on the ice surface

A parameterization of the goal crease's outline. The goal crease is the area where a goaltender plays their position. It is comprised of two components: the outline of the crease, and the filling in its boundary (see documentation for GoalCreaseFill class). The goal crease may have two notches (one on each side of the line y = 0).

crease_length (float): The distance from the center of the goal line to the start of the arc of the goal crease crease_width (float): The exterior width of the goal crease notch_dist_x (float): The distance from the center of the goal line to the notch (if one exists) in the goal crease notch_width (float): The width of the notch (if one exists) in the goal crease crease_style (str): The style of goal crease to implement. Viable options are: nhl98 (the current iteration of the NHL goal crease. This is): what is used for most professional leagues nhl92 (the previous iteration of an NHL goal crease. It is drawn): as a semi-circle with two L-shaped notches at the edge of the crease intersecting the semi-circle ushl1 (the current iteration of a USA Hockey goal crease. This): is what is currently used in the USHL (United States Hockey League)

A parameterization of the goal crease's filling. The goal crease is the area where a goaltender plays their position. It is comprised of two components: the outline of the crease (see documentation for GoalCreaseOutline class), and the filling in its boundary. The goal crease may have two notches (one on each side of the line y = 0).

crease_length (float): The distance from the center of the goal line to the start of the arc of the goal crease crease_width (float): The exterior width of the goal crease notch_dist_x (float): The distance from the center of the goal line to the notch (if one exists) in the goal crease notch_width (float): The width of the notch (if one exists) in the goal crease crease_style (str): The style of goal crease to implement. Viable options are: nhl98 (the current iteration of the NHL goal crease. This is): what is used for most professional leagues nhl92 (the previous iteration of an NHL goal crease. It is drawn): as a semi-circle with two L-shaped notches at the edge of the crease intersecting the semi-circle ushl1 (the current iteration of a USA Hockey goal crease. This): is what is currently used in the USHL (United States Hockey League)

A parameterization of the goaltender's restricted area of a hockey rink. The goaltender's restricted area marks where a goaltender is legally allowed to handle the puck behind the net. This is often referred to as "the trapezoid" as it is trapezoidal in shape. Its line thickness should be given by minor_line_thickness as this is a minor line on the ice surface. NOTE: This is not a requirement in all leagues, and may be omitted via the has_trapezoid key in the rink_params passed to the HockeyRink class

short_base_width (float): The exterior base-width of the trapezoid (should it exist) that along the goal line long_base_width (float): The exterior base-width of the trapezoid (should it exist) that lies along the boards

A parameterization of the faceoff circle at the center of a hockey rink. The center faceoff circle is where the each period of the game begins. It differs from the non-centered faceoff circles in that there are no adjoining hash marks on this circle. It is also a different color than the non-centered faceoff circles. Its line thickness should be given by minor_line_thickness as this is a minor line on the ice surface

A parameterization of the off-centered faceoff circles of a hockey rink. The non-centered faceoff circles are located in the offensive and defensive zones of the ice, with one on each side of the x-axis. These circles differ from the center faceoff circle because they have hash marks that extend towards the boards on each side of the circle

hashmark_width (float): The width of the hashmarks on the exterior of the defensive and offensive faceoff circles. Note that width refers to a distance solely in the y direction hashmark_ext_spacing (float): The exterior horizontal spacing between the hashmarks on the exterior of the defensive and offensive faceoff circles. Note that this is solely in the x direction

A parameterization of the off-centered faceoff spot of a hockey rink. The non-centered faceoff spots are located in the neutral, offensive and defensive zones of the ice, with one on each side of the x-axis. These spots differ from the center faceoff spot because they have a larger diameter, differ in color, and have a colored stripe that runs through its center. This class is responsible for creating the outer ring, not the colored stripe running through it. Please see the documentation for the NODZoneFaceoffSpotStripe class for more information on it

A parameterization of the off-centered faceoff spot of a hockey rink. The non-centered faceoff spots are located in the neutral, offensive and defensive zones of the ice, with one on each side of the x-axis. These spots differ from the center faceoff spot because they have a larger diameter, differ in color, and have a colored stripe that runs through its center. This class is responsible for creating the inner stripe, not the colored outer ring around it. Please see the documentation for the NODZoneFaceoffSpotRing class for more information on it
gap_width (float): The gap between the interior edge of a non-centered faceoff spot ring and the stripe running across it

A parameterization of the faceoff lines in the offensive/defensive zone. These lines are the L-shaped lines where players on each team line up when taking a faceoff in either the offensive or defensive zones. There are four of these faceoff lines around each offensive/defensive faceoff spot

faceoff_line_dist_x (float): The distance from the center of the defensive and offensive faceoff spot to the left-most edge of the upper-right faceoff line faceoff_line_dist_y (float): The distance from the center of the defensive and offensive faceoff spot to the bottom edge of the upper-right faceoff line faceoff_line_length (float): The exterior length of the faceoff line faceoff_line_width (float): The exterior width of the faceoff line over_x (bool): Whether or not the line should be reflected over the x axis over_y (bool): Whether or not the line should be reflected over the y axis

A parameterization of a goal frame. The goal frame is where the puck enters after crossing the goal line to score a legal goal. The front face of the goal is flush with the goal line, while the back edge features rounded corners and expands outside of the front posts. The goal frame is composed of two pieces: the frame (this class) and the fill (see GoalFrameFill documentation)

goal_mouth_width (float): The interior distance between the goalposts goal_back_width (float): The width of the back of the goal frame, measured to the centre of the back pipe: as in sportyR, the drawn frame reaches post_diameter / 2 beyond it on each side goal_depth (float): The depth of the goal frame from the center of the goal line: as in sportyR, the drawn back edge of the frame sits post_diameter in front of it post_diameter (float): The diameter of the posts of the goal frame

A parameterization of the filling of a goal frame. The goal frame is where the puck enters after crossing the goal line to score a legal goal. The front face of the goal is flush with the goal line, while the back edge features rounded corners and expands outside of the front posts. The goal frame is composed of two pieces: the frame (see GoalFrame documentation) and the fill (this class)

goal_mouth_width (float): The interior distance between the goalposts goal_back_width (float): The width of the back of the goal frame, measured to the centre of the back pipe: as in sportyR, the drawn frame reaches post_diameter / 2 beyond it on each side goal_depth (float): The depth of the goal frame from the center of the goal line: as in sportyR, the drawn back edge of the frame sits post_diameter in front of it post_diameter (float): The diameter of the posts of the goal frame

A parameterization of the player bench area's outline for a single team. The player benches are the areas outside the confines of the rink where players not currently on the ice are seated. They are to be on the same side of the ice surface and separate, as close to center ice as possible
bench_length (float): The exterior length of a single team's bench area bench_depth (float): The interior depth off the boards of a single team's bench area

A parameterization of the penalty box for a single team. The penalty boxes are the areas outside the confines of the rink where players serve time for a penalty incurred. They are to be on the same side of the ice surface and separate, as close to center ice as possible, for each team. This will also include the off-ice officials' box

penalty_box_length (float): The interior length of a single penalty box penalty_box_depth (float): The interior depth off of the boards of a single team's penalty box penalty_box_separation (float): The distance that separates each team's penalty box area. This should be equivalent to the length of the off-ice officials' box

A parameterization of the interior of the player bench area. The player benches are the areas outside the confines of the rink where players not currently on the ice are seated. They are to be on the same side of the ice surface and separate, as close to center ice as possible
bench_length (float): The exterior length of a single team's bench area bench_depth (float): The interior depth off the boards of a single team's bench area

A parameterization of the interior of the penalty box for a single team. The penalty boxes are the areas outside the confines of the rink where players serve time for a penalty incurred. They are to be on the same side of the ice surface and separate, as close to center ice as possible, for each team. This will not include the off-ice officials' box; see the documentation for the OffIceOfficialsBox class for more information

penalty_box_length (float): The interior length of a single penalty box penalty_box_depth (float): The interior depth off of the boards of a single team's penalty box penalty_box_separation (float): The distance that separates each team's penalty box area. This should be equivalent to the length of the off-ice officials' box
A parameterization of the interior of the off-ice officials' box. The off-ice officials' box is located between the two penalty boxes, opposite the team bench areas
officials_box_length (float): The interior length of the off-ice officials' box officials_box_depth (float): The interior depth off of the boards of the off-ice officials' box

The default is 0.0 feature_radius (float): The radius needed to draw the feature. This may not be needed for all features. The default is 0.0 feature_thickness (float): The thickness with which to draw the feature. The constraint around the interior edge of the pitch's boundary lines. This confines all interior features to be constrained inside the pitch, as well as any interior plots.

One half, either the offensive or defensive half, of the pitch. This allows each half to take on its own color and be plotted independently, but the halves may take the same color so they look symmetrical

The apron of the pitch beyond the touchline and goal line. This is to allow a more accurate representation of the pitch, as no ads are allowed within a certain distance of the exterior edge of the touchline and goal line
The touchline of the pitch, aka the sideline. These are the lines that run the full length of the pitch
The goal line of the pitch, aka the endlines. These are the lines that run the full width of the pitch. The ball must completely cross the goal line to score a goal
The arc in each corner of the pitch. These are quarter-circles located where the touchline meets the goal line
The halfway line of the pitch, aka the midfield line or center line. This is the line that run the full width of the pitch
The center circle on the pitch. The given radius should be to the outside of the circle.
The penalty box. This is usually the 16.5 m (18 yd) box, but may be parameterized

box_length (float): The length of the penalty box in TV view. This is the larger of the two boxes, and is usually 16.5 m (18 yards) from the back edge of the goal line half_box_width (float): Half the width of the penalty box penalty_mark_dist (float): The distance from the back edge of the goal line to the center of the penalty mark
The goal box. This is usually the 5.5 m (6 yd) box, but may be parameterized

The center mark on the pitch. This is where the kickoffs for each half, as well as following any goal, are taken
The penalty mark. This is the center point for arc of the penalty box, as well as where any penalty kick is taken

The corner defensive marks. These are optional marks on the pitch, located 9.15 m (10 yd) from the corner of the pitch. Defenders should be beyond these marks (either more towards the goal or more towards the halfway line) during corner kicks

is_touchline (bool): Whether or not the corner defensive mark is along the touchline is_goal_line (bool): Whether or not the corner defensive mark is along the goal line depth (float): The depth (in any direction) of the defensive marks beyond the goal line or touchline separation_from_line (float): The distance from the exterior edge of the goal line to the interior edge of the defensive mark

An extension of the BaseFeature class for volleyball features. The following attributes are specific to volleyball features only. For more information on inherited attributes, please see the BaseFeature class definition. The default values are provided to ensure that the feature can at least be created.

court_length (float): The length of the court in TV view. The default is 0.0 court_width (float): The width of the court in TV view. The default is 0.0 feature_radius (float): The radius needed to draw the feature. This may not be needed for all features. The default is 0.0 feature_thickness (float): The thickness with which to draw the feature. This is normally given as the horizontal width of the feature in TV view, however it may be used to specify other thicknesses as needed. The default is 0.0 field_units (str): The units with which the feature is drawn. The default is "ft"
The constraint around the interior edge of the court's boundary lines. This confines all interior features to be constrained inside the court, as well as any interior plots.

The free zone of a volleyball court. This is similar to the court apron of a basketball court in that it is the area outside of the court. It may be the same color as the interior of the court, but isn't necessarily. Unlike a basketball court's apron, however, the boundary line thickness doesn't matter since the lines are considered in-play and therefore are included in the court's length and width.

free_zone_end_line (float): The distance the free zone extends beyond the outer edge of the end line free_zone_sideline (float): The distance the free zone extends beyond the outer edge of the sideline

The front zone of a volleyball court. The front zone is the area between the attack line and the line running along x = 0. If considering the entirety of the volleyball court as being divided into thirds, this is half of the middle third of the court
attack_line_edge_to_center_line (float): The distance from the edge furthest from the attack line to the center of the line running along x = 0

The backcourt area of the volleyball court. This is the area between the attack line and the end line. Players playing in the back row of the rotation must take off from this area before attacking the ball
attack_line_edge_to_center_line (float): The distance from the edge furthest from the attack line to the center of the line running along x = 0

The apron of the volleyball court. The court apron is similar to the court apron of a basketball court in that it is the area outside of the court, but this is different than the FreeZone as it is fully contained within the free zone.

court_apron_end_line (float): The distance the free zone extends beyond the outer edge of the end line court_apron_sideline (float): The distance the free zone extends beyond the outer edge of the sideline
The end lines. These are the lines that run the full width of the court, and their entire thickness is considered in bounds during play
The sidelines. These are the lines that run the full length of the court, and their entire thickness is considered in bounds during play

The attack line. This is the line that runs from sideline to sideline, separating the backcourt from the front zone. Players in the front row may attack from either side of this line, while players in the back row must begin their attack from the backcourt side of this line. The anchor point of this feature should be its outer edge
The center line. This line runs along the line x = 0 when viewing the court in TV view, dividing the court into two equal halves

A single service zone mark. These marks lie beyond the end lines and denote where a legal serve must take place. It appears as a hash mark that is out of bounds of the court, but contained within the free zone
service_zone_mark_length (float): The length of the service zone mark

A single dash of the substitution zone. The substitution zone is typically marked by a dashed line extending from the attack lines. This creates a single dash, and the dashes should be added to the plot accordingly
dash_length (float): The length of a single dash of the service line

surface.binned_stat_2d(x, y, values, statistic = 'sum', xlim = None, ylim = None, binsize = 1, bins = None) Create a two-dimensional binned statistic via scipy. Parameters​ x (numpy.ndarray): A sequence of values to be binned along in the first dimension y: A sequence of values to be binned along in the second dimension values (numpy.ndarray): The data on which the statistic will be computed. This must have the same shape as x, or a list of sequences that each have the same shape as x statistic (str or callable): The statistic to compute via scipy. Per scipy, the following are available: "count": the number of points inside each bin "max": the maximum for points inside each bin "mean": the mean of values for points inside each bin "median": the median for points inside each bin "min": the minimum for points inside each bin "std": the standard deviation for points inside each bin "sum": the sum of the values for points inside each bin {function}: a user-defined function that utilizes a 1-dimensional array of values and outputs a single numerical statistic The default is "sum" xlim (tuple of float or tuple of int): The lower and upper bounds of the x coordinates that should be included. This is only used if the bins argument is None ylim (tuple of float or tuple of int): The lower and upper bounds of the y coordinates that should be included. This is only used if the bins argument is None binsize (float or tuple of float): The size of the bins for any given portion of the surface: a single float: the size of the bins for both dimension a tuple of floats: the size of the bins in each dimension bins (int or tuple of ints or numpy.ndarray or tuple of numpy.ndarray,): optional The specifications of each bin: a single int: the number of bins for both dimensions a tuple of ints: the number of bins in each dimension a numpy.ndarray: the bin edges for both dimensions a tuple of numpy.ndarrays: the bin edges in each dimension Returns​ stat: (nx, ny) numpy.ndarray: The values of the selected statistic in each of the two-dimensional bins x_edge: (nx + 1) numpy.ndarray The bin edges along the first dimension y_edge: (ny + 1) numpy.ndarray The bin edges along the second dimension

A subclass of the BaseSurfacePlot class to make a baseball field. This allows for the creation of the baseball field in a way that is entirely parameterized by the field's baseline characteristics. By convention, TV view for baseball is identical to the view from the high home plate camera. All attributes should default to 0.0 (if of a numeric type) or an empty string (if of a string type). Customized parameters may be specified via a child class (see below) or by directly specifying all necessary attributes of a valid baseball field. The attributes needed to instantiate a particular league's surface must be specified in the field_params dictionary. For many leagues, these will be provided in the surface_dimensions.json file in the data/ subdirectory of sportypy. See the BaseSurfacePlot and BaseSurface class definitions for full details.

league_code (str): The league for which the plot should be drawn. This is case-insensitive but should be the shortened name of the league (e.g. "Major League Baseball" should be either "MLB" or "mlb"). The default is an empty string rotation_amt (float): The angle (in degrees) through which to rotate the final plot. The default is 0.0 x_trans (float): The amount that the x coordinates are to be shifted. By convention, the +x axis extends from the pitcher's plate towards first base when viewing the field in TV view. The default is 0.0 y_trans (float): The amount that the y coordinates are to be shifted. By convention, the +y axis extends from the back tip of home plate out towards center field when viewing the field in TV view. The default is 0.0 feature_colors (dict): A dictionary of coloring parameters to pass to the plot field_params (dict): A dictionary containing the following parameters of the field: field_units (str): The units of the field left_field_distance (float): The straight-line distance from the back tip of home plate to the left field foul pole (along theta = -45°) right_field_distance (float): The straight-line distance from the back tip of home plate to the right field foul pole (along theta = +45°) center_field_distance (float): The straight-line distance from the back tip of home plate to straight-away center field (along theta = 0°) baseline_distance (float): The distance of each baseline running_lane_start_distance (float): The straight-line distance from the back tip of home plate to the start of the running lane running_lane_depth (float): The straight-line distance from the outer edge of the first-base line to the outer edge of the running lane running_lane_length (float): The straight-line length of the running lane measured from the point nearest home plate. As an example, if the base lines are 90 feet, and the running lane starts a distance of 45 feet down the line from the back tip of home plate, and extends 3 feet beyond first base, this parameter would be given as 48.0 pitchers_mound_center_to_home_plate (float): The distance from the center of the pitcher's mound to the back tip of home plate. NOTE: this does not necessarily align with the front edge of the pitcher's plate pitchers_mound_radius (float): The radius of the pitcher's mound pitchers_plate_front_to_home_plate (float): The distance from the front edge of the pitcher's plate to the back tip of home plate pitchers_plate_width (float): The width of the pitcher's plate (the dimension in the y direction) pitchers_plate_length (float): The length of the pitcher's plate (the dimension in the x direction) base_side_length (float): The length of one side of a square base home_plate_edge_length (float): The length of a full side of home plate infield_arc_radius (float): The distance from the front edge of the pitcher's mound to the back of the infield dirt base_anchor_to_infield_grass_radius (float): The distance from the anchor point of a base to the circular cutout in the infield grass. The anchor point of a base is defined as the point used in the definition of the base paths. As an example, in MLB, the anchor point of first base would be the corner of the first base bag along the foul line on the side furthest from the back tip of home plate line_width (float): The thickness of all chalk lines on the field foul_line_to_infield_grass (float): The distance from the outer edge of the foul line to the outer edge of the infield grass foul_line_to_foul_grass (float): The distance from the outer edge of the foul line to the inner edge of the grass in foul territory batters_box_length (float): The length of the batter's box (in the y direction) measured from the outside of the chalk lines batters_box_width (float): The width of the batter's box (in the x direction) measured from the outside of the chalk lines batters_box_y_adj (float): The shift off of center in the y direction that the batter's box needs to be moved to properly align home_plate_side_to_batters_box (float): The distance from the outer edge of the batter's box to the outer edge of home plate catchers_box_shape (str): The shape of the catcher's box. Currently-supported values are: "rectangle" (default behavior) "trapezoid" (see LittleLeagueField for example) catchers_box_depth (float): The distance from the back tip of home plate to the back edge of the catcher's box backstop_radius (float): The distance from the back tip of home plate to the interior edge of the backstop home_plate_circle_radius (float): The radius of the dirt circle surrounding home plate

Customized parameters may be specified via a child class (see below) or by directly specifying all necessary attributes of a valid soccer pitch. The attributes needed to instantiate a particular league's surface must be specified in the pitch_params dictionary. For many leagues, these will be provided in the surface_dimensions.json file in the data/ subdirectory of sportypy. See the BaseSurfacePlot and BaseSurface class definitions for full details.

league_code (str): The league for which the plot should be drawn. This is case-insensitive but should be the shortened name of the league (e.g. "Major League Soccer" should be either "MLS" or "mls"). The default is an empty string rotation (float): The angle (in degrees) through which to rotate the final plot. The default is 0.0 x_trans (float): The amount that the x coordinates are to be shifted. By convention, the +x axis extends from the center of the surface towards the right-hand goal when viewing the pitch in TV view. The default is 0.0 y_trans (float): The amount that the y coordinates are to be shifted. By convention, the +y axis extends from the center of the surface towards the top of the pitch when viewing the pitch in TV view. The default is 0.0 pitch_updates (dict): A dictionary of updated parameters to use for the soccer pitch. The default is an empty dictionary color_updates (dict): A dictionary of coloring parameters to pass to the plot. Defaults are provided in the class per each rule book, but this allows the plot to be more heavily customized/styled. The default is an empty dictionary units (str): The units that the final plot should utilize. The default units are the units specified in the rule book of the league. The default is "default" pitch_params (dict): A dictionary containing the following parameters of the pitch: pitch_length (float): The length of the pitch in TV view pitch_width (float): The width of the pitch in TV view line_thickness (float): The thickness of the lines on the pitch.
